classification.difficultyReason: Check translations by substituting throughout coefficient-sensitive expressions; the exponential comparison also requires an index-law rewrite.

questions.mappingNote: The nine statements test the substitution conventions and coefficient-sensitive transformations demonstrated on these teaching pages.
questions.methodNote: Replace x or y in the original equation for horizontal or vertical translations; simplify afterwards. Use index laws for the exponential comparison.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise translations by substituting into polynomial, logarithmic, square-root and exponential expressions, including coefficients inside the argument.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine an unknown horizontal displacement by comparing logarithmic arguments after substitution.

questions.mappingNote: The unknown horizontal displacement between logarithmic rules follows the comparison method demonstrated for the square-root rules on page 6.
questions.methodNote: Introduce a signed rightward displacement a, replace x with x-a in the original rule, and compare expressions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine an unknown horizontal displacement by comparing logarithmic arguments after substitution.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught horizontal and vertical replacements directly to the two factors of an implicit relation.

questions.mappingNote: The implicit product relation uses the same coordinate-substitution method as the translated circle example on page 5, with the downward substitution established on page 4.
questions.methodNote: Replace x and y throughout the original implicit equation. Horizontal and vertical translations may be applied in either order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the taught horizontal and vertical substitutions directly to an implicit product relation.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret each supplied translation and shift the given curve, including its endpoints, turning points and asymptotes, without changing shape.

questions.mappingNote: Printed 18 and 19 assess horizontal replacement; printed 20 and 21 assess vertical replacement, including endpoints and asymptotes.
questions.methodNote: Use the taught x/y replacement method to translate the entire graph without changing its shape.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch a single horizontal or vertical translation of each supplied graph, preserving its shape and relevant features.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover translations from differently written rules, including completing the square under a radical, then interpret the resulting semicircle and sketch corresponding features.

questions.mappingNote: All four source items assess translations and paired sketches. Individual method mappings are retained on their response leaves.
questions.methodNote: Use coordinate substitution for translations, with characteristic-point comparisons where useful.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify translations and sketch paired curves, including a factored cubic and a semicircle requiring completion of the square.

classification.difficultyReason: Factor the radical's argument to identify a one-unit horizontal shift, then move the supplied endpoint and curve.

questions.mappingNote: Replacing x by x-1 gives sqrt(2(x-1))=sqrt(2x-2). Page 3's coefficient-sensitive radical example directly supports this substitution.
questions.methodNote: A right translation replaces x by x-a throughout the original rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify one horizontal translation of a supplied square-root graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare logarithmic arguments and translate both the curve and its vertical asymptote.

questions.mappingNote: The equation-comparison method on page 6 applies to the logarithmic argument. Matching 2(x-a)+1 with 2x-3 gives a=2, rather than a shift of 4.
questions.methodNote: Use x↦x-a in the original rule, compare expressions and solve for a.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare logarithmic arguments and translate both the curve and its vertical asymptote.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the same horizontal substitution to both numerator and denominator, then preserve both branches and asymptotes.

questions.mappingNote: The numerator 3(x-1)+1 and denominator 2(x-1)-1 simplify to the requested rule. The common substitution establishes a one-unit right translation, including the vertical asymptote.
questions.methodNote: A horizontal translation replaces every occurrence of x by x-a.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the same horizontal substitution to both numerator and denominator, then preserve both branches and asymptotes.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare rational rules to recognise a vertical translation and sketch the resulting branches and asymptotes.

questions.mappingNote: Page 4 teaches vertical replacement; page 7 compares original and translated equations. The rational rules differ by exactly 1, so their graphs differ by a vertical translation.
questions.methodNote: Use vertical coordinate replacement y→y−b, rearrange the translated equation, and compare rules.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare rational rules to recognise a vertical translation and sketch the resulting branches and asymptotes.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise a common replacement across reordered cubic factors, verify it throughout the product, and separate the additional vertical shift.

questions.mappingNote: The factored cubic becomes the target factor product under x↦x+1; replacing y↦y+2 then gives its constant downward shift. This follows the coordinate substitutions demonstrated for combined translations.
questions.methodNote: Translate by replacing x with x−a and y with y−b in the original equation, then compare the resulting rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify both translations by comparing the factors and constant term of cubic expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the combined translation and apply it consistently to the supplied hyperbola's vertices, branches and two oblique asymptotes.

questions.mappingNote: Page 5 translates an implicit circle by replacing both coordinates. The same substitution translates this hyperbola and its asymptotes; page 7 supports comparing defining features.
questions.methodNote: Replace x and y in the original relation to translate it; compare centres or corresponding defining features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate an implicit relation in both coordinates and preserve its branches and asymptotes.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete matching squares in both numerator and denominator to reveal a common horizontal replacement, then translate the supplied maximum and preserve the horizontal asymptote.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 2–3 require replacement of x throughout an expression. Completing both squares reveals x−1, while page 7 supports tracking the maximum as a defining feature.
questions.methodNote: A right translation replaces every occurrence of x by x−a; compare corresponding curve features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise a horizontal translation by completing squares in both parts of a rational expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Split the rational expression to expose an added constant, then shift both branches, turning points and the oblique asymptote vertically.

questions.mappingNote: The extra x in the numerator contributes an additive 1. Writing y−1 equal to the original function applies the substitution method illustrated on pages 3–4.
questions.methodNote: Translate vertically by replacing y, then make y the subject; shift corresponding features by the same vertical displacement.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise an additive constant within a rational expression and translate turning points and an oblique asymptote.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse the stated translations with the correct substitution signs, then expand and collect terms to recover each original implicit relation.

questions.mappingNote: Both printed items belong to the same instruction and remain distinct editable response parts.
questions.methodNote: Use coordinate replacement to translate implicit relations, reversing the stated replacements to recover the original relation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover original implicit relations by reversing the stated coordinate translations and simplifying.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify a translated cubic and use the translation to recover its factorisation.

questions.mappingNote: The general substitution method supplies the translation step; the source question itself establishes the subsequent factorisation dependency.
questions.methodNote: Replace x by x+4 for the left translation. Factor the simpler translated polynomial and reverse the substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify a translated cubic and use the translation to recover its factorisation.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine parameter conditions for prescribed intersection counts after vertical and horizontal translations.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) translates f vertically; part (b) applies the taught horizontal replacement directly. The attached teaching examples do not explicitly demonstrate absolute-value intersection counting.
questions.methodNote: The source teaches translations by replacing x with x-a and y with y-b. The intersection count is established by solving the two branches of the supplied absolute-value function and checking each branch restriction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine parameter conditions for prescribed intersection counts after vertical and horizontal translations.

classification.difficultyReason: Analyse both absolute-value branches as k varies, enforce the restricted domain of g, and distinguish a coincident vertex intersection from loss of a root at the domain boundary.

questions.mappingNote: The restriction belongs to g only. Since an intersection must lie on g, all intersection coordinates must satisfy x>=0. Restricted-domain intersection counting is not explicitly demonstrated in the attached translation examples.
questions.methodNote: Use the source's vertical-translation interpretation, solve the two absolute-value branches, and apply the printed domain restriction of g to the resulting intersections.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine branch validity and a restricted comparison domain to identify all parameter ranges giving one intersection.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover both translations from an expanded implicit hyperbola equation.

questions.mappingNote: The implicit-curve substitution on teaching page 5 supports simultaneous translations; teaching page 7 supplies the coefficient-comparison method for recovering translation parameters.
questions.methodNote: Replace x with x-a and y with y-b, expand, and compare coefficients and the constant term.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover both translations from an expanded implicit hyperbola equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Introduce two translation parameters, expand the mixed xy term correctly, solve the linked coefficient equations and verify the constant term.

questions.mappingNote: Teaching page 5 demonstrates replacement in an implicit quadratic relation; teaching page 7 demonstrates recovering two translation parameters by coefficient comparison.
questions.methodNote: Use simultaneous x/y replacement, expand, equate coefficients, solve the resulting linear equations and check the constant term.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand a translated implicit quadratic relation, solve simultaneous coefficient conditions and verify the constant term.

classification.difficultyReason: Resolve an oblique displacement into equal horizontal and vertical components, then translate a general function.

questions.mappingNote: Resolve the stated displacement into equal components using Pythagoras, then apply the taught replacements to the general function. Component resolution extends the supplied translation examples.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–4 teach coordinate replacement for horizontal and vertical translations. Pages 4–5 explain that their order does not matter.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Resolve an oblique displacement into equal horizontal and vertical components, then translate a general function.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive symbolic displacement components from a slope and distance, then apply them to a general function.

questions.mappingNote: Use the slope relation and Pythagoras to obtain the symbolic components, then follow the taught coordinate-replacement method. The component calculation is an enrichment extension rather than a reproduced worked example.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–5 teach replacement of x and y to combine translations. Pages 6–7 use symbolic translation parameters when comparing curves.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive symbolic displacement components from a slope and distance, then apply them to a general function.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires choosing a translated reciprocal representation for two symbolic rational functions and identifying the coefficient preserved when their asymptotes are aligned.

questions.mappingNote: Rewrite the rational functions to expose their asymptotes and reciprocal coefficients, then compare under the taught horizontal and vertical replacements. This generalises the curve-comparison method; the supplied teaching pages contain no rational-hyperbola worked example.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–5 teach coordinate replacement. Pages 6–7 compare translated rules using symbolic parameters and unchanged curve features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rewrite two symbolic rational hyperbolas and identify the coefficient invariant under horizontal and vertical translations.

classification.difficultyReason: Checks coordinate substitutions in polynomial, rational and implicit equations, including reflections in both axes.

questions.mappingNote: The eleven statements assess the coordinate-substitution rules, function-rule examples, implicit-curve examples and both-axis reflection example on the supplied teaching pages.
questions.methodNote: Replace x with −x for reflection in the y-axis and y with −y for reflection in the x-axis. Replace both coordinates for a 180° rotation about the origin, then simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Checks coordinate substitutions in polynomial, rational and implicit equations, including reflections in both axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare two orders of axis reflections and explain their common result.

questions.mappingNote: Page 14 explicitly compares both orders; page 15 demonstrates simultaneous substitution. These directly support the comparison requested in question 12.
questions.methodNote: Axis reflections act independently. Replace y by −y for an x-axis reflection and x by −x for a y-axis reflection; replacing both gives an origin rotation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare two orders of axis reflections and explain their common result.

classification.difficultyReason: Justify the different effects of a y-axis reflection on shifted even and odd powers.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 12–13 establish the axis substitutions. Page 15 explicitly factors negative cubic brackets, supporting the even-versus-odd comparison.
questions.methodNote: Replace x by −x for reflection in the y-axis, then factor the negative from each bracket and simplify the power. Replace y by −y for reflection in the x-axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Justify the different effects of a y-axis reflection on shifted even and odd powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Show algebraically that the same pair of cubic graphs can be related by both a horizontal translation and an origin rotation.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 14–15 directly support origin rotation and cubic simplification. Earlier translation teaching pages were not supplied; the right-2-unit substitution is supported by the assignment guidance and agrees with the answer evidence.
questions.methodNote: Replace both x and y by their negatives for an origin rotation and factor the negative from the cubic bracket. The translation calculation follows the assignment's prescribed replacement x ↦ x−a.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Show algebraically that the same pair of cubic graphs can be related by both a horizontal translation and an origin rotation.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the coordinate sign changes for reflections in either axis and both axes.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) changes only the output sign; part (b) changes only the input sign; part (c) changes both. The coordinate-labelled reflection examples on pages 15–16 directly support these mappings.
questions.methodNote: Replacing x by -x reflects in the y-axis; replacing y by -y reflects in the x-axis. Applying both changes both coordinate signs, independently of order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the coordinate sign changes for reflections in either axis and both axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the specified axis reflections to supplied curves, tracking intercepts, endpoints and asymptotes and recognising when symmetry makes reflected graphs coincide.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 12 and 14 establish the axis and double-reflection rules. Pages 15–16 demonstrate sketching reflected unspecified functions. Page 13 supports reflection of the logarithmic-shaped graph in item 21.
questions.methodNote: Reflect in the y-axis by replacing x with −x, in the x-axis by replacing y with −y, and in both axes by making both replacements. Reflect corresponding features; either order gives the same double reflection.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply three reflections to six supplied graphs, preserving intercepts, endpoints, symmetry and asymptotic behaviour.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply coordinate substitutions to seven explicit and implicit equations, simplifying even and odd powers, rational expressions and tangent parity.

questions.mappingNote: All seven original items share one instruction requesting the same three operations in a fixed order.
questions.methodNote: Reflect using x→−x and/or y→−y substitutions. A 180° origin rotation applies both substitutions. Simplify only after substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply coordinate substitutions to seven explicit and implicit equations, simplifying even and odd powers, rational expressions and tangent parity.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the appropriate coordinate substitutions from explicit and implicit equations, simplify signs and powers, then map the supplied curves' loops, branches and intercepts.

questions.mappingNote: Individual part records identify the relevant teaching examples and the exact substitutions.
questions.methodNote: Use coordinate substitutions to identify reflections in the x-axis, y-axis or both axes, then map the supplied graph's features.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise coordinate sign substitutions and sketch reflections of explicit and implicit curves, preserving intercepts, endpoints and asymptotes.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that either coordinate sign substitution gives the same transformed implicit equation.

questions.mappingNote: Both substitutions change xy=1 into xy=-1, so the equation does not identify a unique reflection axis.
questions.methodNote: Use coordinate sign substitutions: replace y by -y for reflection in the x-axis and x by -x for reflection in the y-axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that either coordinate sign substitution gives the same transformed implicit equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify an input reflection by substituting -x and handling the signs of three cubic factors.

questions.mappingNote: Input negation alone produces the supplied target rule; therefore the assessed transformation is reflection in the y-axis.
questions.methodNote: Replace the input by its negative, then factor -1 from each cubic factor, as demonstrated in the factored-cubic reflection example.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify an input reflection by substituting -x and handling the signs of three cubic factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the logarithm of a reciprocal to recognise output negation and identify the reflection axis.

questions.mappingNote: The reciprocal logarithm simplifies to -ln x on the original positive domain, identifying reflection in the x-axis.
questions.methodNote: Compare the transformed rule with output negation. The teaching pages distinguish x-axis output negation from y-axis input negation and demonstrate identifying reflections from equations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the logarithm of a reciprocal to recognise output negation and identify the reflection axis.

classification.difficultyReason: Notice that reversing the squared factor leaves it unchanged, exposing a negated output and hence an x-axis reflection.

questions.mappingNote: Because (2-x)^2=(x-2)^2, the requested rule is exactly the negative of the original rule. Page 12 supplies the reflection rule, and pages 14–16 demonstrate identifying a reflection from an equation.
questions.methodNote: Identify the coordinate substitution after simplifying powers: negating the output reflects the graph in the x-axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that reversing a squared bracket leaves its value unchanged and that the remaining output sign change is an x-axis reflection.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply three coordinate-sign substitutions and simplify rational, absolute-value, trigonometric and exponential rules.

questions.mappingNote: All four original printed items share this instruction and remain one editable two-column multipart question.
questions.methodNote: Coordinate-sign substitution produces axis reflections; replacing both coordinates produces a 180° rotation. Simplify after substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply three coordinate-sign substitutions and simplify rational, absolute-value, trigonometric and exponential rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that changing the sine term while retaining the linear factor requires both axis reflections, then transform a nonstandard supplied graph. The source prints a challenge marker.

questions.mappingNote: Page 14 explains that both reflections produce a 180° rotation; page 15 demonstrates simultaneous substitution. Here −f(−x)=x(1−sin x), so reflecting in only one axis would give the wrong requested graph.
questions.methodNote: Combine both axis reflections through simultaneous coordinate-sign substitution, then transform each point of the graph.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that changing the sine term while retaining the linear factor requires both axis reflections, then transform a nonstandard supplied graph. The source prints a challenge marker.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise both axis reflections from a change to the cosine term while preserving the linear term, then transform the supplied increasing curve. The source prints a challenge marker.

questions.mappingNote: The both-axes explanation on page 14 and simultaneous-substitution example on page 15 apply directly. Cosine evenness gives −f(−x)=x+cos x.
questions.methodNote: Use both coordinate-sign substitutions to obtain the requested equation, then rotate the supplied graph through 180°.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise both axis reflections from a change to the cosine term while preserving the linear term, then transform the supplied increasing curve. The source prints a challenge marker.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise both coordinate reflections from a polynomial rule and identify their equivalent rotation.

questions.mappingNote: Page 14 explicitly identifies the equivalent rotation; page 15 demonstrates replacing both coordinate signs in a polynomial equation. These methods produce the target rule.
questions.methodNote: Reflect in the y-axis by replacing x with −x and in the x-axis by replacing y with −y. Both reflections together give a 180° rotation about the origin.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise both coordinate reflections from a polynomial rule and identify their equivalent rotation.

classification.difficultyReason: Derive a reflected exponential rule, simplify a negative exponent and prove a functional identity.

questions.mappingNote: The substitution follows the rule on page 12 and the function-rule example on page 13. Simplifying the negative exponent gives a common denominator for the requested identity.
questions.methodNote: For a reflection in the y-axis, replace x with −x to obtain g(x)=f(−x), then simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Derive a reflected exponential rule, simplify a negative exponent and prove a functional identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply successive reflections to a rational function and solve for the intersection coordinates of the original and transformed graphs.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 14–15 establish the combined sign substitution and independence of the reflections. Equating the two resulting rational rules uses ordinary algebra to find the requested intersections; the supplied teaching pages contain no worked intersection example.
questions.methodNote: Replace y with −y for the x-axis reflection and x with −x for the subsequent y-axis reflection, giving g(x)=−f(−x).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply successive reflections to a rational function and solve for the intersection coordinates of the original and transformed graphs.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply reflections to both branch formulas and their restrictions, reversing inequalities under negative-input substitution and keeping each rule attached to its transformed domain.

questions.mappingNote: Question 50 applies these substitutions separately to both pieces. The horizontal reflection also acts on each branch restriction and reverses its inequality.
questions.methodNote: Use the source substitutions y to -y for reflection in the x-axis and x to -x for reflection in the y-axis. Both substitutions may be made simultaneously.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reflects both branches of a piecewise function and reverses their domain inequalities under a y-axis reflection.

classification.difficultyReason: Form the double reflection and connect a unique intersection with paired opposite x-values; logarithmic domain restrictions and the supplied parameter target guide the proof and intersection coordinates.

questions.mappingNote: Question 51 uses the same direct substitution to obtain g, then equates f and g. The logarithmic domains establish b>0 and validate the single-intersection argument.
questions.methodNote: The logarithmic example substitutes -x into the original argument. Reflection in both axes additionally negates the output; the order of the reflections does not matter.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses logarithmic laws and domain restrictions to interpret exactly one intersection after reflection in both axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect the reflected exponential intersection equation to a positive-variable quadratic or reciprocal-sum minimum, using positivity to distinguish the parameter giving exactly one intersection.

questions.mappingNote: Question 52 uses y=-f(-x) for the reflected exponential rule. Equating the rules and substituting t=2^x reduces the single-intersection condition to a repeated positive quadratic root.
questions.methodNote: Replace both x and y by their negatives to reflect in both axes, retaining the source order of x-axis then y-axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reflects an exponential function in both axes and uses a positive-variable substitution and repeated-root condition to find a parameter.

classification.difficultyReason: Reframe a symbolic rational hyperbola around its asymptotes, show that double reflection preserves its reciprocal coefficient, and derive the equivalent translation and conditions for an axis-only displacement.

questions.mappingNote: Page 12 gives the axis-substitution rules; pages 13–16 demonstrate their application to explicit and implicit equations and reflections in both axes. Question 53 extends that method to comparing rational hyperbolas under translation; these pages do not supply a worked translation-comparison example.
questions.methodNote: Reflect by replacing y with -y and x with -x. For a function this gives g(x)=-f(-x); simplify before comparing with a translated rule.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare a rational hyperbola with its reflection in both axes and determine parameter conditions for horizontal and vertical translations.

classification.difficultyReason: Read each input coefficient and take its reciprocal using the taught horizontal dilation convention.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess horizontal dilation factors, including reciprocal fractional coefficients.
questions.methodNote: Use the taught substitution x ↦ x/k. Page 22 explicitly demonstrates that a factor of 1/3 gives the input 3x. The excluded example on page 24 correctly obtains h=1/2, but its final sentence incorrectly says the dilation factor is 2; the reciprocal convention on pages 21–22 governs these solutions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identifies horizontal factors by expressing each input as x divided by the factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Isolate y where necessary and read the resulting output multiplier as the vertical dilation factor.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b read the output multiplier directly; parts c–d first isolate y to determine that multiplier.
questions.methodNote: Vertical dilation replaces y by y/k, giving y=kf(x). Page 22 demonstrates rearranging the equation after a vertical substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identifies vertical factors, with rearrangement required when y has a coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify which coordinates measure distance from the named axis or origin and multiply those coordinates by two.

questions.mappingNote: Dilation from the x-axis is vertical, dilation from the y-axis is horizontal, and dilation from the origin scales both coordinates.
questions.methodNote: Page 21 identifies the unchanged coordinate for horizontal and vertical dilations. Page 22 defines dilation from the origin as applying the same factor horizontally and vertically.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies a scale factor to the coordinate perpendicular to an axis or to both coordinates from the origin.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires justification that two different coordinate dilations produce the same quadratic.

questions.mappingNote: The output multiplier 9 equals the square of the input multiplier 3, so vertical factor 9 and horizontal factor 1/3 give the same quadratic.
questions.methodNote: Compare replacement of y by y/k with replacement of x by x/h, using the reciprocal horizontal factor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires justification that two different coordinate dilations produce the same quadratic.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose input substitution or output multiplication for each stated dilation, then simplify the resulting rational expression using the taught method.

questions.mappingNote: Page 22 demonstrates these substitutions and rational-function simplification. Each of the four parts applies the corresponding substitution to x/(x+2).
questions.methodNote: For a horizontal dilation replace x by x/k; for a vertical dilation replace y by y/k and rearrange.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply horizontal and vertical reciprocal substitutions to a rational function and simplify.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply reciprocal substitutions to an implicit circle equation, including squared scale factors.

questions.mappingNote: The page-23 vertical-dilation example starts with the identical unit-circle equation. Page 21 supplies the horizontal and vertical substitution rules used by all four parts.
questions.methodNote: Substitute x/k or y/k into the original implicit equation, then simplify the squared expression.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply reciprocal substitutions to an implicit circle equation, including squared scale factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Use horizontal and vertical substitutions to obtain new polynomial and rational-function equations.

questions.mappingNote: Individual mappings to the polynomial and rational-function examples are retained on the four response leaves.
questions.methodNote: Apply x/k for horizontal dilation or y/k for vertical dilation, then simplify the resulting equation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use horizontal and vertical substitutions to obtain new polynomial and rational-function equations.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify reciprocal horizontal and direct vertical scale factors, combine them on the labelled points, and preserve the curve's shape when sketching.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply a single coordinate scaling. Parts c and d combine independent horizontal and vertical scalings. The supplied labelled points, rather than an inferred function equation, determine each sketch.
questions.methodNote: Horizontal dilation by k replaces x with x/k and maps (x,y) to (kx,y). Vertical dilation by l replaces y with y/l and maps (x,y) to (x,ly). Apply both coordinate scalings when both input and output multipliers occur.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch horizontal, vertical and simultaneous dilations of a supplied graph, transforming its labelled intercepts and minimum.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret input multipliers reciprocally and combine horizontal and vertical scaling while retaining the supplied curve's intercepts and two turns.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) scales x by 4; part (b) scales y by 1/2; part (c) rewrites 2x/3 as x/(3/2) and scales x by 3/2; part (d) scales x by 2 and y by 3. These mappings follow the horizontal, vertical and simultaneous coordinate substitutions demonstrated on the inspected teaching pages.
questions.methodNote: Horizontal dilation factor k replaces x by x/k and multiplies point x-coordinates by k. Vertical dilation factor l replaces y by y/l and multiplies point y-coordinates by l. Apply both substitutions for combined dilations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch horizontal, vertical and combined dilations of a supplied graph, preserving intercepts and turning-point topology.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that both changed y terms arise from the same substitution y to 2y, then halve vertical coordinates throughout the supplied two-branch curve.
